# CountDownLatch

A `CountDownLatch` lets one or more threads wait for a set of signals from other
threads. This is useful when a coordinator must wait for several independent
tasks, such as initialisation work, before proceeding.

This example starts three workers and uses a latch with a count of three. Each
worker signals once; the main thread can return normally from `await()` when all
three signals have reduced the count to zero. The latch is one-shot: it cannot
be reset for another round.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this example, attendees can:

- explain how `countDown()` and `await()` coordinate a one-shot completion
  signal;
- identify the visibility guarantee provided by a successful `await()`; and
- distinguish a signal from successful task completion and handle the
  limitations of interruption and an unfinished worker.

## Prerequisite

Install an
[Oracle Java 8](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/downloads/#java8) JDK
or newer and ensure `java` and `javac` resolve to it in the terminal running
this example.

## The program to inspect

Each worker simulates work and calls `countDown()` in a `finally` block. If the
worker enters that block, it signals even when the simulated work fails; the
latch does not report whether the work succeeded. A worker that never reaches
`countDown()`, including one stuck in its work, can leave the main thread
waiting indefinitely. The latch counts signals, not thread termination, and does
not stop or join the workers.

If `await()` is interrupted, the main thread restores its interrupt status and
logs the exception. It then also logs that all workers have signalled, even
though this may be false. Treat that final message as evidence of completion
only when `await()` returns normally; an application must handle interruption
without making that assumption.

```java
final CountDownLatch latch = new CountDownLatch(3);

// Create and start three worker threads
for (int i = 1; i <= 3; i++) {
    final Runnable task = () -> {
        log("Task is performing some work before signaling its completion");

        try {
            /* Simulate some work with the resource */
            sleepForTwoSeconds();
            log("Task completed; counting down the latch.");
        } finally {
            latch.countDown();
        }
    };

    new Thread(task, "Thread-" + i).start();
}

log("Main thread is waiting for tasks to finish...");
try {
    latch.await(); /* Main thread waits until the latch count reaches zero */
} catch (final InterruptedException e) {
    Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
    logError("Main thread interrupted while waiting for the other threads to complete.", e);
}
log("All workers have signalled completion. Main thread can proceed.");
```

## Relation to the Java Memory Model (JMM)

The JMM defines rules for visibility and ordering of shared state. The
`CountDownLatch` API specifies that, until the count reaches zero, actions
before a thread calls `countDown()` happen-before actions after a successful
return from the corresponding `await()` in another thread. Thus, the main thread
can observe worker updates made before their signals after a normal return from
`await()`. This example does not exchange shared results, so its output does not
demonstrate that visibility guarantee.

The latch does not make concurrent updates by workers atomic or provide mutual
exclusion. Sleep simulates work; neither it nor log timing establishes the
happens-before relationship. The order of worker logs is scheduling-dependent.

## Guided walkthrough

Run these commands from the `examples/count-down-latch` directory. Choose one of
the following ways to run the example. In a normal, uninterrupted run, each
worker logs its work before signalling, and the main thread proceeds after all
three signals. Worker log order and timing vary between runs.

1. Run the example using the
   [Maven `exec` plugin](https://www.mojohaus.org/exec-maven-plugin/).

   ```shell
   ./mvnw clean compile exec:exec
   ```

   One possible run; task and log ordering will vary.


2. Build the application and create the JAR file.

   ```shell
   ./mvnw clean package
   ```

   (*Optional*) List the created JAR file.

   ```shell
   tree --dirsfirst --sort=name './target/libs'
   ```

   The application JAR file

   ```
   └── count-down-latch-1.0.0.jar

   1 directory, 1 file
   ```

   Run the application.

   ```shell
   java \
     -classpath './target/libs/*' \
     demo.Main
   ```
